country.comment: Single-city case study of Hyderabad (Andhra Pradesh) situated within national Indian urban water policy reforms.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, and Introduction; PDF p. 4, Table 1

effect_estimate.comment: Primary analysis is qualitative; numeric figures reported in the paper are descriptive statistics synthesized from secondary municipal reports and prior household surveys rather than primary causal/statistical estimates by the author.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Institutional analysis and fieldwork show that decentralization under the 1992 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, donor-driven cost-recovery/PPP policies, and utility customer-service reforms (Single Window Cell, Metro Customer Care, Citizen's Charter) improved service interaction for registered middle- and upper-income consumers while largely excluding unrecorded slum residents. Secondary descriptive figures synthesized in the study indicate that despite reported network coverage of 95% citywide and 90% in slums (with only ~40% of meters functioning), low-income areas receive intermittent water for only a few hours on alternate days; 70-80% of water subsidies in India fail to reach the poor lacking metered connections; unconnected slum households pay 2 to 20 times more per liter to tankers/vendors; shared connections push low-income multi-household users above the subsidized <12 Rs/kL tariff blocks (up to 30 kL/month); and poorer households spend ~4% of income on water versus 0.7% among richer households.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 1, 3-6, Abstract, The Urban Water Regime in Hyderabad, and Discussion

mechanism_certainty.comment: Qualitative institutional case study appraised with CASP (design ceiling = 2). Directly documents how administrative rules, customer registration boundaries, utility reforms, municipal notification, and increasing block tariff structures operate to exclude or penalize low-income slum households in accessing affordable piped water.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 2, 4-6, Methodology, The managerial aspect, The social aspect, and Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines legal/administrative eligibility of notified slums and exclusion of unrecorded consumers (tenure), JNNURM/CDP urban renewal and nonmandatory rainwater harvesting planning (planning), increasing block tariffs, subsidy targeting, and full-cost recovery (fees), Single Window Cell connection application processing and computerization barriers (procedural_steps, delay), Metro Customer Care grievance handling and Charter obligations (complaint), multi-level governance split across federal/state/municipal agencies under the 74th CAA (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination), and poor residents' exclusion from decision-making alongside citizen coalition/social-movement participation (participation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, ENFORCEMENT, tenure, planning, fees, procedural_steps, delay, complaint, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 1, 2, 4-7, 10, Introduction, Table 1, The managerial aspect, The social aspect, Discussion, and Endnote [1]

outcome_flags.comment: Examines piped household and metered network connections (formal_connection), poor households' water access (water_access), citywide and slum coverage rates (service_coverage), intermittent alternate-day supply and frequency (service_continuity), sufficiency and pressure of supply (service_quantity), potability/purity, filtering, and waterborne illness (service_quality), tariff/vendor prices and income share spent on water (affordability), and connection/service delivery delays (delay).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary empirical component is qualitative fieldwork (15 in-depth interviews, narrative walks, and in situ observation) integrated with qualitative policy/document analysis; quantitative numbers cited in the text are secondary descriptive statistics from prior studies and municipal reports rather than a primary quantitative component, making CASP Qualitative Checklist the appropriate tool.

sample_size.comment: Primary empirical fieldwork consisted of 15 in-depth interviews (plus narrative walks and in situ observation) across 3 Hyderabad slum areas in January 2011; the author also extracted secondary data from government policy/CDP documents and two prior Hyderabad surveys mentioned in Methodology.
sample_size.value: 15 in-depth interviews with residents across 3 slum areas (primary fieldwork); also synthesizes secondary survey data from Raghavendra 2006 (550 households) and Davis et al. 2008 (919 households across 14 notified slum areas)

study_design.comment: Qualitative single-city governance case study framed by the multi-level perspective (MLP) from transition studies, triangulating policy/document review, secondary published survey/municipal statistics, and primary qualitative interviews, narrative walks, and observation.
study_design.value: Qualitative case study (multi-level perspective transition analysis combining policy/legislative document analysis, synthesis of secondary household survey and municipal data, and primary fieldwork with structured open-ended interviews, narrative walks, and in situ observation)

evidence_quotes.quote: In January 2011, I conducted two weeks of intensive fieldwork in disadvantaged urban areas of Hyderabad and carried out 15 in-depth interviews with residents of the three slum areas of Jagadgirigutta in Quthbullahpur, Fathenagar in Kukatpall, and Secunderabad Division in Begumpet towns.

The maintenance of central control through regulation and funding by the federal and state governments, the inadequate capacity to perform decentralized functions effectively by local governance, and the continued exclusion of the poor from influence over the decisions affecting their welfare, are among the main obstacles and issues associated with decentralization and institutional changes implemented by the 74th CAA

evidence_quotes.criterion: effect_estimate / mechanism_flags (registered consumer requirement, procedural reforms)
evidence_quotes.quote: Although these initiatives have increased the ability of users to interact with the HMWSSB effectively, they are too focused on registered consumers (Joshi 2007). This excludes the urban poor in slum areas who are neither recorded consumers nor are served by providers.

evidence_quotes.criterion: effect_estimate / outcome_flags (affordability, increasing block tariff on shared connections)
evidence_quotes.quote: On the other hand, users sharing only one connection end up paying more per kilo-liter since higher blocks of the water tariff are not subsidized creating a situation where individual users in low-income areas pay more for water while receiving less (Whittington 2003, Raghavendra 2006, HMWSSB 2008).

evidence_quotes.criterion: mechanism_flags (tenure / legal entitlement of notified slums)
evidence_quotes.quote: Notified slums are those that are notified by a municipality and other local authorities and are legally entitled to the provision of basic services from the government.
